name: Schools of Emotion
description: The constellation root for Recursive Repatterning. Every branch below is a family of traditions for making sense of feeling. None of them is presented as the discovery of a fixed biological truth about emotion; the constructionist account — that there are no fixed biological fingerprints for discrete emotions — is the substrate this whole library sits on, not one branch among the others. The branches are not a survey of the field and could not be: this is a handful of the ways people have organised feeling, chosen and built one at a time. An empty branch is left visible on purpose, as a placeholder for work not yet done rather than something hidden.

attribution.name: PlayfulProcess
attribution.note: Author of this constellation grammar and its branch descriptions. No text is copied from any school's own copyrighted sources here - each branch note is original commentary describing what kind of tradition belongs there, not quoting from it.

_note: Generated by scripts/build_constellation.py from schools/_collection.json — do not hand-edit the items. To change what the constellation shows, edit the branches in _collection.json (their names, notes and school_slugs) or the school's own grammar, and rebuild. The top-level name, description, tags and attribution below ARE hand-authored and are passed through untouched.

sections.What it is: This is not a peer school. Every other grammar in this collection presents a tradition's own taxonomy of emotion in its own terms; this one is different in kind. The theory of constructed emotion, developed chiefly by psychologist and neuroscientist Lisa Feldman Barrett and collaborators, is the frame the whole library sits inside — the working premise stated in this project's own CLAUDE.md: there are no fixed biological fingerprints for discrete emotions, and people still have to make meaning, so every taxonomy elsewhere in this collection is a usable map, not a discovery of natural categories. On this account, an emotion is not a triggered, pre-packaged program with one fixed signature; it is an instance constructed in the moment from core affect (a continuously varying background sense of how pleasant/unpleasant and how activated one currently is), interoceptive signals from the body, and a learned concept — itself shaped by language and culture — that the brain applies to categorize the whole pattern as "anger," "joy," or whatever word fits. This grammar exists so the substrate has its own drawable items like every other school, not to establish it as one option among equals.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'growing'. The theory of constructed emotion has a substantial and actively growing body of peer-reviewed empirical support — the 2019 Barrett/Adolphs/Marsella/Martinez/Pollak meta-analysis on facial-expression variability, cross-cultural work with low-media-exposure populations (Gendron et al. 2014), and a developing predictive-processing/interoception research program — but it is a comparatively recent paradigm still being actively tested against, and argued over with, basic-emotion accounts, rather than a claim treated as independently settled across the field. "Growing" reflects a real and expanding evidence base under live contestation, not an unsettled or merely theoretical claim.

metadata.deck: Constructed Emotion — the Substrate

sections.What this branch is: Not a peer school. This is the frame the whole library sits inside: emotions have no fixed biological fingerprints, so every taxonomy below is a meaning-layer, not a discovery.

sections.What it is: A three-position oracle deck exploring the recursiveness of life. Each card sits in one of three positions: Structure (what constrains and holds), Process (what moves and constructs), Possibility (what opens when the process overflows). Together they form the recursive spiral — the ethics of constructivism as a practice you can deal.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'theoretical'. This is the library's own constructed account, not a tradition curated from elsewhere — a set of practice-cards built from a working synthesis of Barrett's constructed-emotion theory, Kashmir Śaivist līlā/recognition doctrine, and the maintainer's own ethics-of-fiction grammar. The tier measures one thing only: transferable, third-person evidence, and by that measure this school has none — no trials, no replication, no peer review — so it sits at 'theoretical' beside the least-evidenced schools it collects, exactly as the library's discipline requires. But the tier does not measure the other kind of warrant, and honesty cuts both ways: a practice can be fully warranted for its practitioner by lived experience in context, without that warrant transferring to anyone else. That is not a loophole; it is what individuation means, and it is consistent with the substrate this library stands on — context reaches all the way down (under stress the same meal yields the body a different result), so a first-person synthesis tested daily in its own context is evidenced in the only way such a thing can be. Paul Brunton, one of the maintainer's teachers, distrusted group religious work for a kindred reason: each person must come to their own understanding, in their own context. So the honest statement is double — this school carries the maintainer's experiential warrant in full, and offers visitors none they do not earn in their own practice.

metadata.deck: Overflow — Structures, Process, Possibilities

items.name: The Ethics of Fiction — A Grammar for Judging Stories

sections.What it is: An ethics of fiction judges stories by what they do, not what they say — by fruits, not doctrine. Generativity is never a property of a story alone: it is a property of a casting — story times context times receiver. Four branches grow from one trunk: Lenses (ways of judging), Contexts (soils a story can be cast into), Cases (worked examples, verdicts-in-progress), and Synthesis (what the judging is for). The load-bearing beam under all of it: does this story, cast in this context, increase or decrease the freedom of the one who receives it?
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'theoretical'. This is the library's own constructed account, not a tradition curated from elsewhere — an ethics-of-fiction instrument built by the maintainer from Tolkien's 'On Fairy-Stories', Wayne Booth's The Company We Keep, Le Guin's Carrier Bag Theory, and other named sources, synthesized into one grammar with its own vocabulary (Lenses, Contexts, Cases, Synthesis, the Freedom Test). It has not been tested, replicated, or peer-reviewed as a method; its own Growth card says its authority 'is only as good as its willingness to be re-cast.' Marking it 'theoretical' — the same tier this collection gives its least-evidenced curated schools — is the whole point: a library whose founding claim is that meaning-making categories are constructed cannot exempt its own maker's construction from that same discipline.

metadata.deck: The Ethics of Fiction — A Grammar for Judging Stories

sections.What this branch is: The library's own synthesis — Overflow (structure, process, possibility, and the recursion between them) and the Ethics of Fiction (judging stories by their fruits, in their casting). First-person where every other branch is curatorial. Its evidence tier is 'theoretical' because tiers measure transferable third-person evidence, and it claims none — but it carries a different warrant the tiers cannot see: lived experience in its own context, which is what individuation means. A made meaning, held visibly as made, and worked daily by its maker.

items.name: Untranslatables — Where Feeling-Words Don't Cross Languages Cleanly

sections.What it is: Words for feeling that do not translate cleanly into English, and the reverse: places where English carves a distinction that other languages do not draw the same way. Each item here states a gap, not a discovery of a hidden universal — what the nearest English terms cover, and what is left over once they're used. The working discipline is Anna Wierzbicka's: an emotion word from any language, English included, is a culturally specific concept, not a culture-neutral box waiting to be filled by different vocabularies. Eduardo Viveiros de Castro's method of controlled equivocation supplies the sharper warning this school is built around — the danger in cross-linguistic work is not failing to find a match, it is assuming a rough gloss is an identity. Both are treated at length in docs/GENEALOGY-OF-EMOTIONS.md Part C.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'observational-only'. That these specific lexical gaps exist — that saudade, Sehnsucht, toska and the rest lack a single clean English equivalent, and that English grief does not map cleanly onto Portuguese — is well documented across dictionaries, linguistics and the primary literary and scholarly sources cited item by item in this school. What any individual gap means — what it implies about the people who use the word, about emotional experience being different rather than differently labeled, about which culture's vocabulary is richer — is interpretive, and Wierzbicka's warning against treating any language's emotion words as a neutral measuring instrument applies to this school doubly: it is the risk this whole school exists to examine, not a risk confined to the schools it points at.

metadata.deck: Untranslatables — Where Feeling-Words Don't Cross Languages Cleanly

sections.What this branch is: What carries between languages, and what does not. Saudade beside longing and landing on neither; English grief distributed across luto, pesar, tristeza and saudade; and the empirical trace — 45 of this library's own words absent from a 400,000-word English model. The gaps are documented; every claim about what a gap means stays interpretive, per Wierzbicka's warning, which applies to this branch doubly.

items.name: Neuroscience of Emotion — Where Feeling Lives in the Body

sections.What it is: This school is different in kind from every other branch in this library. Where Plutchik, NVC, DBT, Aquinas, or rasa each propose a taxonomy of what the significant emotional categories are, this school asks a different question entirely: where, physically, in nervous tissue has feeling been located — and by what evidence? From the 1930s onward, researchers proposed that specific brain structures and closed anatomical circuits implement specific emotions: the amygdala as a fear centre, the insula as a disgust centre, a Papez circuit and later a whole 'limbic system' as emotion's dedicated hardware. This grammar holds that localisationist picture faithfully, in its own terms, alongside the meta-analytic evidence that has substantially revised it — including a reversal by the very researcher most responsible for establishing the amygdala-fear link. Both halves are presented here: what was reasonably believed and taught for decades, and what a large pooled body of neuroimaging evidence now shows. Neither collapses into the other.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'observational-only'. This tier describes the school's classic, organizing content — the five region-emotion mappings and the Papez/limbic-system/triune-brain architecture — which rest on individually real but non-selective lesion and neuroimaging studies rather than confirmed, specific, one-to-one findings; several of its central claims (limbic system as a bounded category, triune brain, amygdala as fear-specific) are now treated by the field as superseded rather than merely contested. This is the unusual case in this library where the CORRECTING evidence is the stronger side: Lindquist et al.'s 2012 meta-analysis (no discrete regional locus for any emotion category) is a well-replicated, independently converging finding drawn from a large pooled literature, and LeDoux's own revision of the amygdala-fear claim came from the researcher who built that claim in the first place. 'Observational-only' is assigned to the root because it must describe the school's organizing content as a whole, which is still substantially the classic picture most readers bring to it — not because the corrective half is itself weakly evidenced. Read each classic-mapping item's own evidence_note for where a specific claim's standing differs from this root-level tier.

metadata.deck: Neuroscience of Emotion — Where Feeling Lives in the Body

sections.What this branch is: Accounts that explain feeling by its implementation in nervous tissue — which region, which circuit, which network. No other branch here asks that question: constitution asks what a person is made of, expression asks how feeling is shown, the basic-emotion schools ask how it is sorted.

sections.What it is: Robert Plutchik's 1980 psychoevolutionary model of emotion, adapted here for adult, oracle-style use. Eight primary emotion families - joy, trust, fear, surprise, sadness, disgust, anger, and anticipation - sit in four opposing pairs, each admitting a mild, moderate, and intense form (apprehension to fear to terror). Adjacent families blend into eight named dyads (love, submission, awe, disapproval, remorse, contempt, aggressiveness, optimism). Draw a card as a vocabulary prompt for naming what you're already feeling, not as a diagnosis of what you must be feeling.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'theoretical'. Plutchik's eight-family structure, its opposite pairs, and its dyad adjacencies are a theoretical proposal with no independent empirical confirmation. The 2019 Barrett/Adolphs/Marsella/Martinez/Pollak meta-analysis found no reliable facial or physiological fingerprint for discrete emotion categories generally, which undercuts the basic-emotion premise this wheel depends on.

metadata.deck: Plutchik's Wheel of Emotions

sections.What it is: The basic-emotion model, developed from the 1960s onward and associated chiefly with Paul Ekman's cross-cultural research programme (though Carroll Izard, Silvan Tomkins, and others contributed independently), holds that a small set of discrete emotions — most commonly anger, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, and surprise, with contempt sometimes added later — are each driven by an evolved "affect programme": a fast, largely involuntary, coordinated pattern of facial muscle movement, physiology, and action tendency, triggered by a specific class of situation and recognizable across cultures. This school is titled by the tradition rather than by a living researcher's name (Paul Ekman is living as of this writing); the model is also strongly associated with the Facial Action Coding System (FACS), a detailed anatomical scheme for describing facial muscle movement that Ekman and Wallace Friesen developed to measure expressions objectively.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'observational-only'. The model's central empirical claim — cross-cultural universality of a small set of discrete facial expressions — rests on cross-cultural judgment studies that are genuinely observational and correlational rather than settled experimental fact: the original forced-choice studies (Ekman & Friesen 1971 and others) reported strong cross-cultural recognition; later studies using free-labeling methodology with populations having less media exposure (Gendron, Barrett, et al. 2014, the Himba) reported substantially weaker agreement; and a 2019 meta-analysis (Barrett, Adolphs, Marsella, Martinez, & Pollak) found no reliable one-to-one facial signature for discrete emotion categories across the wider literature. This school does not adjudicate that dispute — evidence_tier reflects that the underlying studies are real and published, not that the universality claim they are cited for has been independently confirmed.

metadata.deck: Basic-Emotion / Affect-Programme Theory

sections.What this branch is: Discrete, evolutionarily-primary categories: a small fixed set of emotions, with blends and intensities built out of them. Plutchik's wheel and Ekman's basic-emotion programme both work this way and still name different sets, which is itself worth noticing.

sections.What it is: Nonviolent Communication (NVC), the communication framework developed by Marshall Rosenberg from the 1960s onward, treats feelings not as verdicts about other people ("you make me angry") or as fixed inner objects to be diagnosed, but as signals pointing toward a need that is either met or unmet in the present moment. A feeling word, on this model, is information — frustration points toward an unmet need (autonomy, perhaps, or effectiveness), relief points toward a need that has just been met (ease, or safety). NVC practice pairs a feelings vocabulary with a needs vocabulary and trains people to move fluently between them, rather than staying at the level of judgment or blame. There is no single, official, universally agreed feelings-and-needs list: Rosenberg's own books present illustrative lists that changed across editions, and the Center for Nonviolent Communication (CNVC), certified trainers, and independent NVC organizations (BayNVC among others) each publish their own versions, overlapping heavily but not identical in wording or grouping.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'growing'. NVC has an expanding body of applied and practitioner-reported evidence (workplace, mediation, education, couples contexts) and increasing academic interest, but a comparatively thin base of independently replicated controlled outcome studies isolating NVC's specific mechanisms from those of adjacent communication and conflict-resolution training it shares territory with. This is a live, growing evidence base, not yet an independently-replicated one in the strict sense.

metadata.deck: Nonviolent Communication — Feelings and Needs

sections.What this branch is: Feelings read as signals of a met or unmet need rather than as categories in themselves — so what a feeling raises is the question of what it points to, not what it should be called. Nonviolent Communication is the school here.

sections.What it is:
Attachment theory is the research tradition John Bowlby began from the late 1950s onward, drawing partly on ethology, to explain why infants form strong, specific bonds to a caregiver and what happens to their behavior when that bond feels threatened. Bowlby proposed an innate attachment behavioural system: under threat, distress, or fatigue, an infant is driven to seek proximity to a specific attachment figure, who serves both as a safe haven (comfort when distressed) and a secure base (the confidence to explore when not). Mary Ainsworth gave the theory its central empirical tool, the Strange Situation — a structured laboratory procedure of brief separations and reunions — and, from what she observed infants doing at reunion, described patterns of attachment now commonly called secure, anxious, and avoidant, with a fourth pattern, disorganised, added later by Mary Main and Judith Solomon. Bowlby's related concept of internal working models describes how repeated experience with a caregiver becomes an internalized template for what to expect from close relationships going forward — revisable, on his account, not fixed for life.

This grammar carries Bowlby and Ainsworth's own descriptive and empirical tradition — the research base the other couple-focused schools in this library draw from in different measure. Sue Johnson's Emotionally Focused Therapy and John and Julie Gottman's Gottman Method, elsewhere in this library, each apply and extend pieces of this theory to adult couples in their own way and are cross-linked here; this grammar itself stays with Bowlby and Ainsworth's own claims, not either therapy's application of them.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'independently-replicated'. Attachment theory's descriptive core — the Strange Situation paradigm and the resulting infant classifications — is among the most independently replicated findings in developmental psychology, reproduced across many independent laboratories over several decades. What is genuinely more contested: how universal the classification distributions are across cultures (large cross-cultural reviews find broadly similar orderings but also real variation that some researchers read as culturally shaped rather than fixed); how well adult self-report and interview measures of attachment actually converge with each other and with infant classification; and how strong the continuity is from infant classification to adult relationship patterns, which longitudinal research finds to be real but modest, not the fixed, deterministic through-line popular accounts sometimes imply. 'Independently-replicated' describes the classification and the paradigm; its extensions into adult attachment and lifespan continuity carry more genuine uncertainty than that tier alone would suggest.

metadata.deck: Bowlby and Ainsworth — Attachment Theory

items.name: Emotionally Focused Therapy — Attachment Bonds Between Partners

sections.What it is:
Emotionally Focused Therapy (EFT) is the couples-therapy model developed by Sue Johnson from the 1980s onward, building on adult attachment theory: the idea that partners in a committed relationship are each other's primary source of emotional safety, and that most recurring couple conflict is really a protest about that safety being in doubt — 'Are you there for me?' EFT reads a couple's conflict cycle, commonly a pursue-withdraw pattern, as two people each defending against the same underlying fear of disconnection in opposite, self-reinforcing ways. Therapy works to de-escalate the cycle, help each partner access the softer, more vulnerable ('primary') emotion they are protecting with a faster, more visible ('secondary') reaction, and restructure their interactions around new, safer responses to each other's attachment needs.

A necessary disambiguation, since the same three letters name two different things in couple and individual therapy: this grammar is Sue Johnson's Emotionally *Focused* Therapy for couples, built on attachment theory. It is a different person and a different model from Leslie Greenberg's Emotion-Focused Therapy, an individual, experiential approach with its own separate lineage. The two are easy to conflate by acronym alone; they are not the same tradition, and neither is a variant of the other.

This grammar carries Sue Johnson's own voice and evidence base only. It draws on attachment theory (Bowlby and Ainsworth, elsewhere in this library) and addresses much of the same couple territory as John and Julie Gottman's Gottman Method, elsewhere in this library; both are cross-linked here, but per this library's one-source-per-grammar rule, their own claims live in their own grammars, not stacked into this one.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'independently-replicated'. Emotionally Focused Therapy has the strongest independent evidence base of the three couple-focused traditions split out of this library's original relationship-cards seed. A 1999 meta-analysis (Johnson, Hunsley, Greenberg & Schindler) pooling multiple randomized controlled trials found large effect sizes for EFT relative to waitlist controls, and subsequent outcome and follow-up studies — run by research teams beyond Johnson's own — have generally supported those gains holding over time. This is why EFT earns 'independently-replicated' rather than 'growing': its core therapeutic claims have been tested and supported outside the tradition's own institute, not only within it.

metadata.deck: Emotionally Focused Therapy — Attachment Bonds Between Partners

sections.What it is:
The Gottman Method is the couples-therapy approach built by John Gottman and Julie Schwartz Gottman from four decades of direct observation of real couples — videotaped conversations, heart-rate and hormone monitoring, and long-term follow-up — conducted first at the University of Washington's 'Love Lab' and later through the Gottman Institute. Rather than starting from theory, the method starts from pattern: watching what actually distinguishes couples who stay together and grow closer from couples who drift apart or divorce, then naming what was observed. Four such patterns turned out to predict relationship trouble with notable reliability — the Four Horsemen of criticism, contempt, defensiveness, and stonewalling — each paired with a specific antidote the Gottmans also observed working in stable couples. Other findings from the same body of research describe what keeps a relationship resilient: bids for connection and how partners respond to them, the balance of positive to negative interaction during conflict (sentiment override), how couples navigate the conflicts that never fully resolve, and a willingness to be moved by a partner's perspective.

This grammar carries the Gottman Method's own voice and evidence base only. It draws on the same territory — couple conflict, connection, and repair — as Sue Johnson's Emotionally Focused Therapy and Bowlby and Ainsworth's attachment theory, elsewhere in this library, and is cross-linked to both; but per this library's one-source-per-grammar rule, those traditions' own claims live in their own grammars, not stacked into this one.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'growing'. The Gottman Method rests on an unusually large and long-running observational and physiological research base — videotaped conflict conversations, heart-rate and hormone data, and follow-up assessments across multiple couple cohorts studied since the late 1970s — which supports its descriptive claims (the Four Horsemen, bids, sentiment override) reasonably well. The intervention side is thinner: most outcome trials of the Gottman Method itself have been conducted or sponsored by the Gottman Institute and its own researchers, and the independent, non-institute replication base for the method's therapeutic effectiveness is smaller than for some other approaches in this library. 'Growing' — not yet 'independently-replicated' — is the honest tier here: a substantial and serious evidence base, with a real gap between how well-replicated the observational findings are and how independently tested the therapy outcomes built on them are.

metadata.deck: The Gottman Method

sections.What this branch is: Feeling as something that happens between people rather than inside one. Bowlby and Ainsworth's research tradition, and the two couples methods that draw on it — kept as separate schools because they are separate bodies of work with genuinely different evidence behind them.

items.name: Dialectical Behavior Therapy — Acceptance and Change Skills

sections.What it is: Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), after Marsha Linehan's published work from the late 1980s onward, organizes a skills-training curriculum around a single structural claim: acceptance and change are not opposites to choose between but two poles that have to be held together at once. The word "dialectical" names that stance directly — a thesis (things are acceptable exactly as they are) and an antithesis (things need to change) are synthesized rather than resolved in favor of one side. DBT's skills training divides into four modules. Mindfulness supplies the foundation — the capacity to notice what is actually happening, inside and outside, before doing anything about it. Distress tolerance and emotion regulation split the acceptance/change axis most visibly: distress tolerance is largely acceptance-oriented (how to survive a crisis, or a moment that cannot yet be changed, without making it worse), while emotion regulation is largely change-oriented (how to shift an emotional response that doesn't fit the facts or isn't working). Interpersonal effectiveness applies the same dialectic to relationships — getting what you want, keeping the relationship, and keeping your self-respect are three goals that can conflict, and part of the skill is naming which one a given interaction is actually for. DBT was developed originally for adults with chronic suicidality and self-harm meeting criteria for borderline personality disorder, and has since been adapted for a wider range of populations and presentations.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'independently-replicated'. DBT has one of the stronger independent evidence bases in this library. Its original claim — that DBT reduces self-harm and suicide attempts and improves treatment retention, relative to comparison conditions, in adults with chronic suicidality and borderline personality disorder — rests on randomized controlled trials beginning with Linehan et al. (1991) and replicated across multiple research groups independent of Linehan's own lab, which is what earns the independently-replicated tier here rather than a weaker one. What is weaker: that evidence is for full, multi-modal DBT (individual therapy, skills group, phone coaching, and a therapist consultation team, run together), not for any single module or skill taught on its own — a standalone skills-training class, of the kind this grammar's items describe, has a thinner and more mixed evidence base than the complete program, and has not been shown to reliably match full-model outcomes by itself. DBT has also been extended well past its original population — to adolescents, eating disorders, substance use, and general emotion dysregulation — and while a number of those extensions have supportive trials, that evidence is generally newer, smaller in volume, and less independently replicated than the original self-harm/BPD indication. The tier reflects that DBT's central claim has real, independent trials behind it, not that every skill or every extension carries that same weight on its own.

metadata.deck: Dialectical Behavior Therapy — Acceptance and Change Skills

sections.What this branch is: Skills taught as a curriculum — acceptance and change held together, practised deliberately rather than arrived at. Linehan's DBT.

items.name: Ericksonian Hypnotherapy — the Conversational Trance and Its Lineage

sections.What it is:
Milton Erickson (1901–1980) rebuilt clinical hypnosis around a simple reversal: trance is not a strange condition imposed by an authority, it is an everyday state — absorption in a story, a drive, a memory — that a skilled conversation can deepen and put to work. Where the older stage tradition commanded ("you are getting sleepy"), Erickson suggested indirectly, through stories, metaphor, ambiguity, and permissive language, and he treated whatever the patient brought — including their resistance — as material to use rather than an obstacle to overcome. He called that principle utilization, and it is the closest thing this school has to a creed.

This grammar holds the method in Erickson's own terms, and then holds the lineage — because Erickson's influence runs far beyond hypnotherapy proper. Strategic family therapy, solution-focused brief therapy, neuro-linguistic programming, and the mass-audience human-needs coaching built on NLP are all, in different ways, Erickson's descendants, and they did not inherit equal shares of his clinical care or of the evidence. This school says which is which.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'growing'. Clinical hypnotherapy carries genuine but domain-specific support (best for pain and IBS; moderate for smoking cessation), and Ericksonian hypnotherapy specifically has a 2025 meta-analysis of eight RCTs showing large effects versus inactive controls and parity with active treatments — a real but small trial base, hence 'growing' rather than 'independently-replicated'. The tier applies to the clinical hypnotherapy only. Two descendants held inside this grammar sit below it: NLP's distinctive claims have repeatedly failed controlled tests, and the human-needs coaching tradition has no independent outcome research — 'theoretical' by this library's tiers — so this school's evidence note is itself an example of the library's founding point: an undifferentiated badge over this lineage would be a false statement.

metadata.deck: Ericksonian Hypnotherapy — the Conversational Trance and Its Lineage

sections.What this branch is: Schools that change feeling by arranging experience rather than explaining it — trance, suggestion, and the state-first premise that insight follows change instead of causing it. Erickson's conversational hypnotherapy is the school here, held together with its unequal heirs: strategic family therapy, solution-focused brief therapy, NLP, and the mass-audience human-needs coaching built on all of it. The branch exists partly to say out loud that those descendants did not inherit equal evidence.

items.name: Parts Work — after Internal Family Systems

sections.What it is:
Parts work treats what feels like a single, unified self as a working system of parts — inner voices, each formed for a reason, each carrying its own memory, role, and protective intention. No part is the enemy. A part that criticizes, that panics, that overworks, that shuts down — each one took on that job at some point because it seemed to work, and none of them are the whole of who you are. Underneath or alongside the parts, this tradition holds there is a steadier quality often called Self: not another part fighting for control, but a capacity for curiosity, calm, and compassion that can be with any part without needing to fix, silence, or become it. The central move this tradition teaches is captured in a phrase common across parts-work practice: get curious, not merged — when a part takes over completely ("blending"), the practice is to notice that, and find enough distance to ask what the part is protecting, rather than either obeying it or fighting it.

This school is adapted primarily from the architecture of Richard Schwartz's Internal Family Systems (IFS) model — parts, Self, protectors (managers and firefighters), and exiles — written here in original prose, not drawn from IFS's own copyrighted training materials, session protocols, or specific terminology set. "Internal Family Systems" and "IFS" are trademarks of the IFS Institute; nothing here should be read as an IFS-branded or IFS-certified resource. No part described here is a diagnosis — this is a way of naming an inner experience, not a clinical assessment of it.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'growing'. Internal Family Systems has a small but expanding base of peer-reviewed outcome research (for example, a controlled trial for rheumatoid arthritis-related distress, and further studies in trauma and other clinical contexts) and was previously included on SAMHSA's National Registry of Evidence-Based Programs and Practices. This is real but limited independent replication compared to longer-established, more heavily studied therapies — "growing" rather than "independently-replicated" is the honest tier here, and much of the model's specific claims still rest on clinical case material rather than controlled research.

metadata.deck: Parts Work — after Internal Family Systems

sections.What it is:
Carl Jung's theory of archetypes: recurring, cross-culturally patterned figures and dynamics that Jung held to structure the collective unconscious, a layer of the psyche he distinguished from both ordinary consciousness and an individual's own personal unconscious. An archetype, in Jung's account, is not a fixed image but a predisposition to organize experience around a pattern — the Shadow, the Anima and Animus, the Self — patterns Jung argued appear independently across unrelated mythologies, dreams, and religious systems because they are inherited structures of the psyche itself, not because one culture borrowed from another. This school covers a working selection of Jung's archetypes, several of the dynamics between them, and the individuation process Jung held those dynamics serve: becoming, not perfecting, oneself.

Jung died in 1961; his Collected Works remain in copyright, as does the later archetypal-psychology and mythological scholarship (James Hillman, Marie-Louise von Franz, Joseph Campbell) that informs this school's selection and framing. No text is quoted from any of these authors anywhere in this grammar — every definition below is this library's own original prose, paraphrasing the concept, not reproducing anyone's wording.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'theoretical'. Jungian archetype theory has never been demonstrated as a claim about inherited psychic structure by genetics, neuroscience, or any other independent empirical discipline — it remains a theoretical and interpretive framework, argued through case material, dream analysis, and comparative mythology rather than through controlled research. Its considerable influence has been clinical, literary, and cultural rather than experimental; this library takes no position on whether archetypes are "real" in Jung's own strong sense, and presents the model as a symbolic vocabulary rather than as a validated psychological finding.

metadata.deck: Jungian Archetypes — The Collective Unconscious

sections.What this branch is: Accounts that treat a person as made of parts, or a feeling as the surface of something with its own aim underneath it — internal-family-systems parts work, and Jung's archetypal psychology.

items.name: The Four Humours — Galenic Temperament Theory

sections.What it is: The longest-running account of feeling in the Western record: from Hippocratic writers in the 5th century BCE through Galen's systematization (2nd century CE) to its dominance in European medicine through the 18th century, the body was held to run on four fluids — blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm — whose relative balance produced both momentary illness and a person's durable temperament. This is a genuinely different kind of account from every other school in this library: it explains feeling by bodily constitution, not by cognition, expression, or need. A temperament here is not a mood that passes; it is closer to what modern usage calls a personality — a standing disposition a humoral excess produces and holds in place for a lifetime. The physiology is discredited: there is no blood/bile/phlegm balance underlying mood, and bloodletting to correct it caused real harm. The vocabulary nonetheless survived the theory that produced it — English speakers still call someone "sanguine," "phlegmatic," "melancholic," or "good-humoured" without any commitment to Galen's physiology, a rare case of a scientific model outliving its own falsification by centuries because the words it minted turned out to be useful for something else.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'theoretical'. Galenic humoral theory is a discredited physiological model: no fluid balance of the kind it describes exists, and the four humours do not correspond to any coherent modern biochemical category. It is retained here as the longest-running historical account of feeling in the Western record and as the direct source of vocabulary (sanguine, choleric, melancholic, phlegmatic) still in ordinary use — a historical and linguistic claim, not an empirical one, and it should not be read as a live physiological hypothesis.

metadata.deck: The Four Humours — Galenic Temperament Theory

items.name: Alchemical Correspondences — Fludd, Paracelsus, and the Opus

sections.What it is: The alchemical and Neoplatonic-emblematic tradition read inner states through a cosmology of correspondence: planets, metals, elements, and stages of the Great Work (magnum opus) were held to map onto one another and onto the human temperament, so that a person's disposition could be described in the same vocabulary as a planet's character or a metal's properties. Robert Fludd (1574-1637), whose 1617 engraving Integrae naturae speculum artisque imago is this library's own homepage image, built an entire encyclopedic cosmology on this principle in his Utriusque Cosmi Historia. Paracelsus (1493-1541) reoriented alchemy toward medicine, treating the alchemist's transformation of matter and the physician's treatment of the body as versions of the same work. Neither offers an empirical account of emotion in any modern sense — this is a symbolic and cosmological system, read here for what it is: an unusually developed vocabulary of inner and transformative states, which is exactly the kind of material this library collects, whatever one makes of the cosmology built around it.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'theoretical'. Alchemical correspondence cosmology is a symbolic and cosmological system, not an empirical one — it offers no testable physical mechanism and no measurement, and this library takes no position on its metaphysical claims. Its interest here is as a highly developed, historically influential vocabulary of inner and transformative states, not as a scientific account of emotion; assessing it by empirical standards would be a category error the tradition itself did not intend, though it is worth naming plainly (unlike, say, a modern psychological model) that no empirical confirmation was ever the tradition's own aim.

metadata.deck: Alchemical Correspondences — Fludd, Paracelsus, and the Opus

items.name: Thought-Forms — Besant, Leadbeater, and the Coloured Aura

sections.What it is: The Theosophical and Anthroposophical account of feeling as visible form and colour: not a state inferred from behaviour, but something claimed to be directly perceived, by trained clairvoyant sight, as coloured shapes in and around the body. Annie Besant and C. W. Leadbeater's Thought-Forms (1901) is the central text — a published key pairing specific colours with specific feelings (affection, devotion, anger, fear, jealousy, and more), illustrated with plates the authors presented as records of particular observed instances rather than as invented art. Leadbeater's Man Visible and Invisible (1902) extends the same colour scheme to the standing aura. Rudolf Steiner's account of the astral body as the seat of feeling grew out of the same Theosophical milieu but diverged from it, in both method and cosmology, on his way to founding Anthroposophy. Neither offers an empirical account of emotion in any modern sense; this library reads the material for what it is — an unusually literal vocabulary for inner states, one that claims a feeling has a shape and a colour that could in principle be drawn.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'theoretical'. Besant and Leadbeater's colour key, and Steiner's parallel account of the astral body, rest on a clairvoyant and visionary claim, not an empirical one: the perceptions described are not independently verifiable, and no controlled test has ever supported clairvoyant aura perception. This is stated plainly, without contempt for the tradition — its interest to this library is as an unusually developed and unusually literal vocabulary for inner states, one that claims feeling has a shape and colour precise enough to draw, not as a scientific account of what emotion physically is.

metadata.deck: Thought-Forms — Besant, Leadbeater, and the Coloured Aura

sections.What this branch is: Accounts that explain feeling by what a person is made of and where they sit in a larger order — humours, elements, planets, stages of an opus — rather than by cognition, expression, or category. Filing these under historical-scientific would misdescribe them: the alchemical tradition never claimed to be empirical, and humoral theory was the medicine of its day rather than a psychology.

items.name: Darwin — The Expression of the Emotions

sections.What it is: Charles Darwin's The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals (1872) argues that human emotional expressions are not arbitrary or divinely designed signals but evolved, largely involuntary residues of once-functional behavior, continuous with expressions in other animals. Darwin builds the case on three explanatory principles — serviceable associated habits (an expression that once served a direct purpose, like baring teeth to bite, persists as a habit even when the purpose no longer applies), antithesis (an opposite emotional state produces a bodily posture that is the physical opposite of the first, even where that opposite posture serves no independent purpose of its own), and the direct action of the nervous system (some expressions, like trembling in fear, are simply what an overloaded nervous system does, with no communicative function at all) — and on evidence he gathered himself: photographs (making this the first psychology text illustrated photographically), direct observation of infants, the insane, and animals, and a questionnaire he circulated to missionaries, colonial officials, and travelers across multiple continents asking whether specific expressions appeared the same in the populations they knew. The book is in the public domain.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'observational-only'. Darwin's evidence — his own direct observation of infants and the institutionalized, comparative observation of animal behavior, and a cross-cultural questionnaire circulated through missionary and colonial contacts — is genuinely empirical for its period but methodologically pre-experimental: no controlled conditions, no standardized stimuli, untrained lay observers, and (in the questionnaire) leading questions asked of colonial-era informants under a power relationship this school does not sanitize. It is a historically foundational observational record, not evidence meeting modern experimental or cross-cultural methodological standards, and it should not be read as settling the same universality questions that later, more rigorous studies (and their critics) continue to dispute.

metadata.deck: Darwin — The Expression of the Emotions

items.name: Affektenlehre — the Baroque Doctrine of the Affections

sections.What it is: Affektenlehre ("doctrine of the affections") is the explicit 17th–18th century Baroque theory that music does not merely accompany or soothe feeling but represents specific, nameable affects through specific, nameable technical means — a key, a bass pattern, a rhythmic figure, a rhetorical device. Johann Mattheson catalogued distinct affective characters for individual musical keys in Das neu-eröffnete Orchestre (1713); Athanasius Kircher's Musurgia Universalis (1650) proposed a fuller physiological-and-cultural account of how music moves the affects; the musica poetica tradition running from Joachim Burmeister through Kircher and Christoph Bernhard catalogued named rhetorical figures, each conventionally carrying its own affective charge; Monteverdi explicitly theorized and claimed credit for a new musical device — the stile concitato — built to represent rage and warfare; and Descartes's early Compendium musicae (1618, decades before his Passions de l'âme) argued that rhythm and interval themselves excite specific passions. This school belongs in this library on its own terms, not as a footnote to the others: it is a taxonomy of feeling built for a genuinely non-verbal medium, something no other school gathered here can claim about its own working material. A period listener, hearing a descending chromatic bass line, could recognize "lament" without a single word being sung — that is the specific, checkable claim Affektenlehre makes, and no other framework in this collection makes an equivalent claim about its own medium.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'theoretical'. Affektenlehre is a historical compositional and rhetorical doctrine — a set of conventions Baroque composers and theorists built, taught, and debated among themselves — not an empirical claim about how listeners actually respond to music, then or now. No controlled study of period or modern listener response is claimed anywhere in the surviving primary sources this school describes; the tradition's authority rests on theoretical treatises and compositional practice, not on experiment.

metadata.deck: Affektenlehre — the Baroque Doctrine of the Affections

items.name: Acting Traditions — How Performers Are Taught to Show Emotion

sections.What it is: Every theatrical tradition that has ever tried to make an audience read grief, rage, or joy off a performer's body has had to codify expression — and each has codified it differently, in a system that has to be explicitly learned. Bharata's abhinaya assigns fixed hand positions and involuntary bodily signs to named states; Noh drills a performer for years to read as sorrow or joy through the tilt of a mask that itself never changes; Charles Le Brun taught 17th-century painters an explicit rule for the eyebrow; François Delsarte charted the body into expressive zones and drilled them into a generation of American and European actors; jingju assigns a color and pattern to a face before the performer ever puts it on. That is the school's argument, stated plainly: if emotional expression were a fixed biological readout, it would not need teaching, and every tradition would teach the same thing. Neither is true. This is empirical support for this library's constructionist substrate coming from centuries of practice rather than from the laboratory — evidence of a kind the lab literature cannot supply. It is not the whole case: actors also exploit real regularities (several of these traditions converge on the eyebrows and the eyes independently), and the traditions overlap rather than contradict each other outright. Two 20th-century traditions, Stanislavski's and Strasberg's, are included specifically because they reject the codified-external premise the other traditions share — the school is stronger for holding a live disagreement, not a settled consensus.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'theoretical'. Every tradition in this school is a working performance practice, refined by trial and audience response over years or centuries, not a controlled empirical study of what emotion is or how it is produced in the body. Their authority rests on demonstrated success at being legibly read by trained and untrained audiences alike within their own convention — a real and checkable kind of success, but a different and weaker warrant than a laboratory finding about the nature of emotion itself. That a system works to communicate a feeling to an audience is not the same claim as that system having discovered what the feeling underneath actually is, and this school does not treat the two as equivalent.

metadata.deck: Acting Traditions — How Performers Are Taught to Show Emotion

items.name: Hasta Mudrā — The Hand-Gesture Vocabulary of Classical Indian Dance

sections.What it is: The Nāṭyaśāstra and, later, Nandikeśvara's Abhinaya Darpaṇa ("Mirror of Gesture") catalogue a drilled, named repertoire of hand positions used in classical Indian dance and dance-theatre — roughly 28 single-hand (asaṃyuta) and 24 joined-hand (saṃyuta) hastas, each with a fixed shape and a list of things it may be used to mean, its viniyoga. This school states its argument plainly: a hasta's meaning is not fixed the way a code's is. A single gesture can carry many different, sometimes unrelated meanings depending on context — pratākā alone signifies clouds, an oath, a blessing, a forest, and the word "stop," among dozens of other things — and a single meaning (the moon, say) can be carried by more than one gesture. The mapping is many-to-many and resolved only by context: by the song, the narrative moment, and the accompanying facial and bodily abhinaya. That is a markedly different model of expression from a code in which one signal reliably means one thing, and it is the reason this school belongs in a library about how feeling gets made rather than found. `schools/acting-traditions` already covers Bharata's four modes of abhinaya (āngika, vāchika, āhārya, sāttvika) as one item in a wider survey of codified performance traditions; this school does not restate that ground and instead begins where it stops, inside āngika abhinaya's actual gesture vocabulary. `schools/rasa` documents what a successful performance does for a qualified spectator; this school does not re-argue rasa theory, only cross-links to it. Read honestly, hastas are communicative signs within a performance grammar — closer to a lexicon a dancer learns than to a display of felt emotion. A dancer whose hands show śṛṅgāra through the appropriate hastas need not personally feel desire in that moment, the same performer/audience distinction schools/rasa already draws for the aesthetic event a hasta helps produce.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'theoretical'. The Abhinaya Darpaṇa and the Nāṭyaśāstra's āngika chapters document a living performance-practice vocabulary, refined and transmitted within trained dance lineages over centuries, not an empirical claim about how emotion is produced or read in the body. A hasta's authority rests on its continued, checkable use and legibility within a specific dance tradition's own convention, not on experimental confirmation of any inner state it may be used to signify — the same distinction schools/acting-traditions draws for its own codified-external systems.

metadata.deck: Hasta Mudrā — The Hand-Gesture Vocabulary of Classical Indian Dance

sections.What this branch is: Accounts concerned with how feeling is shown or conveyed — in the face and body, in a gesture lexicon, or in the conventions of an art — rather than with what it is made of or how it is categorised. Darwin, the Baroque doctrine of the affections, the acting traditions and the hasta vocabulary all ask the same question in different media.

items.name: Greek Pathē — Rhetoric and Stoic Ethics

sections.What it is: Two adjacent, non-identical Greek frameworks gathered under one school because both use the word pathē (πάθη, roughly "that which is undergone") and both come out of the same fourth-to-third-century BCE philosophical culture in Athens — not because they agree with each other. Aristotle's Rhetoric (Book II) catalogues pathē as states a speaker can arouse in an audience to make a case land: they are appraisals bound to a rhetorical situation (who feels this, toward whom, and on what belief), not a clinical inventory of inner states. The Stoics, from Zeno and Chrysippus onward, use pathē in a stricter and more critical sense — an irrational, excessive impulse that follows from a false judgment about what is good or bad, which the wise person replaces with a calibrated "good feeling" (eupatheia) rather than simply having less of. Treating Aristotle's rhetorical pathē and Stoic ethical pathē as one undifferentiated "Greek emotion theory" flattens a real disagreement between them about what pathē even are.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'theoretical'. Both frameworks are philosophical argument, not empirical research — the Rhetoric is a handbook for persuasion and the Stoic pathē scheme is an ethical claim about which judgments are true. Neither offers, or claims to offer, cross-cultural or physiological evidence; assessing them by that standard would be a category error the traditions themselves did not intend.

metadata.deck: Greek Pathē — Rhetoric and Stoic Ethics

sections.What it is: René Descartes's Les passions de l'âme (The Passions of the Soul, 1649) proposes that every passion of the soul, however complex, is a combination or degree of six primitive ones: wonder (admiration), love (amour), hatred (haine), desire (désir), joy (joie), and sadness (tristesse). These six are not Paul Ekman's twentieth-century "basic emotions" wearing older dress — they predate that model by more than three centuries, arrive by a wholly different method (introspective philosophical analysis plus Descartes's own mechanistic physiology of "animal spirits" moving through the body and pineal gland), and answer a different question: not which facial expressions are cross-culturally recognized, but which passions cannot be built out of any others. Descartes wrote for a physician's and a princess's eyes (the treatise grew out of his correspondence with Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia) rather than for a laboratory.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'theoretical'. Descartes reached his six primitives by philosophical introspection combined with a since-superseded mechanistic physiology, not by empirical measurement of any kind. No cross-cultural or experimental evidence was collected or claimed; the taxonomy stands or falls as philosophical argument, not as a scientific finding.

metadata.deck: Descartes's Six Primitive Passions

sections.What it is: Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologiae (Prima Secundae, questions 22–48, written c. 1270) sorts eleven passions of the sensitive appetite into two faculties: six concupiscible passions (love/hatred, desire/aversion, joy/sorrow) and five irascible passions (hope/despair, fear/daring, and anger, which Aquinas holds has no contrary). The organising line between the two faculties is not good-versus-bad — both faculties handle both good and evil objects. It is arduousness: the concupiscible appetite responds to a sensory good or evil simply apprehended as such; the irascible appetite responds to that same good or evil only insofar as it is arduous — difficult to attain, difficult to escape, or requiring struggle to reach or resist. A passion Aquinas calls hope is not simply modern-English "hope": it is, specifically, the appetite's movement toward a future good that is both possible and hard to get.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'theoretical'. Aquinas's eleven-passion taxonomy is a work of scholastic philosophical psychology, derived by argument from Aristotelian and Avicennian premises about the soul's powers, not from observation or experiment. No empirical support is claimed by the tradition itself, and none should be inferred here.

metadata.deck: Aquinas's Eleven Passions

sections.What it is: The Nāṭyaśāstra, a Sanskrit treatise on dramaturgy attributed to Bharata Muni (compiled roughly between the 2nd century BCE and 2nd century CE), names eight rasas — śṛṅgāra, hāsya, karuṇa, raudra, vīra, bhayānaka, bībhatsa, adbhuta — and the philosopher-aesthetician Abhinavagupta added a ninth, śānta, in his 10th–11th century commentary. A rasa is not a feeling a character has, and not a feeling a spectator merely catches by contagion. It is an aesthetic event that arises between a well-executed performance (built from vibhāva, the determinants; anubhāva, the consequents; and vyabhicāribhāva, the transitory states) and a qualified spectator's own aesthetic relish (āsvāda) of the sthāyibhāva, the stable emotional theme, that the performance has made tastable. Calling rasa "the Indian emotion list" collapses that relational, performance-dependent structure into the same fixed-inner-state model this whole library exists to question — rasa is closer to a claim about what good theatre does than to a claim about what feelings exist inside a body.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'theoretical'. Rasa theory is a work of dramaturgical and aesthetic philosophy developed and debated within the Sanskrit commentarial tradition over more than a millennium (Bharata through Abhinavagupta and beyond). It is not an empirical psychological theory and does not claim cross-cultural or physiological evidence; its authority within its own tradition rests on argument and on continued use by practitioners, not on experimental confirmation.

metadata.deck: Rasa — Bharata's Aesthetics of Performance

items.name: Qíng and the Seven Emotions — Classical Chinese Medicine

sections.What it is: Classical Chinese medical theory, systematized in texts descending from the Huangdi Neijing (Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic, compiled roughly 2nd century BCE – 2nd century CE) and elaborated through later medical writing, names qīqíng — seven emotions — and links five of them to the five zàng (yin viscera): the heart governs joy (xǐ), the liver governs anger (nù), the spleen governs pensiveness/overthinking (sī), the lung governs grief (bēi, often paired with yōu, worry), and the kidney governs fear (kǒng). This is not a psychology in the Western sense grafted onto medicine; it is medicine — emotion is one of several categories of pathogenic factor (alongside diet, climate, and overexertion) capable of injuring qì circulation and, in excess or over time, the organ each is paired with. The word this school translates loosely as "emotion," qíng (情), has a semantic range wider than the English word: across Chinese philosophical and medical usage qíng can mean felt emotion, but also disposition, circumstance, the true state of a thing, or human feeling in general — treating qíng as a one-to-one synonym for "emotion" narrows a term that classical sources use more broadly.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'theoretical'. The five-viscera emotion correspondences are a theoretical framework internal to classical Chinese medicine's Five Phases cosmology, transmitted and elaborated over roughly two millennia of textual and clinical tradition. They are not supported by, and do not claim to be supported by, controlled biomedical evidence in the modern sense; their standing here is as a historically significant and still clinically active framework, not as an independently replicated empirical finding.

metadata.deck: Qíng and the Seven Emotions — Classical Chinese Medicine

sections.What it is: How the unit of analysis itself — what counts as one feeling, how many there are, what axis organizes them — has been rebuilt independently by five traditions that mostly did not know of one another's work: Greek/Latin-Christian/European philosophy and psychology, Sanskrit dramaturgical aesthetics, Chinese classical medicine, Amazonian perspectivist ethnography, and Micronesian ethnopsychology. Each lineage is followed on its own terms, in its own internal chronology, rather than folded into one timeline with a single spine. Draw on this deck as a map of moments, not a single spine of progress toward a correct list.
sections.Evidence: Held at evidence tier 'theoretical'. This root item's own claim is interpretive: that reading five independent traditions' histories together supports treating emotion categories as constructed rather than discovered. It aggregates five lineages whose own internal evidence tiers differ (theoretical for Greek/Sanskrit/Chinese, observational-only for Amazonian/Micronesian) and does not average or launder those differences into one rating.

metadata.deck: A Genealogy of Emotions

sections.What this branch is: The long record of the question before there was a discipline to ask it in, and the map of how those answers connect: Aristotle's rhetorical pathē and the Stoic four, Aquinas's eleven passions, Descartes's six primitives, Bharata's rasa, and the seven qíng of classical Chinese medicine — five traditions that asked what a feeling is and did not arrive at the same answer — together with the genealogy grammar that traces the lineages between them.

sections.What this is: The constellation as it currently stands: 28 schools in 13 branches, sitting on a constructionist substrate rather than on any one branch's claim to have found emotion's true shape. This is a handful of the ways people have organised feeling, not a catalogue of them — the library could not hold them all, and does not claim to. Open a branch to see its schools; open a school to draw from it directly.
